```
The command then proposes its edits as a diff (one hunk shown) and lists what it deliberately left alone: the refund window, the tone requirement, and the quality bar. You review a patch, not a rewrite.
Anthropic measured the effect on a support-desk evaluation 14 , across two migrations between earlier models:
- From Claude Opus 4.8 to Claude Opus 5, prompts written for the older model cost more per ticket on the newer model, for no change in accuracy.
- Running the audit over the same prompts made Claude Opus 5 both cheaper than the unaudited version and more accurate, a gain outside the noise.
- From Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Claude Sonnet 5, the audit cut the cost per ticket at the same accuracy.
The two kinds of stale text have different costs:
- Instructions the new model follows too literally cost money: removing "verify twice" cut Claude Opus 5's cost per ticket, and removing "be maximally thorough" cut it almost as much.
- Text that no longer fits the model costs accuracy instead: a retired thinking setting, contradictory rules, and a hand-rolled scratchpad that conflicts with the model's own thinking each restored accuracy on Claude Opus 5 when removed.
The same patterns tend to appear in tool descriptions and skills, which are worth auditing too.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Trade cost against intelligence 
text:
## Trade cost against intelligence 
These levers set where a single model sits between cost and intelligence: model choice, effort, re-running failures at a higher setting, the budgets and caps it works within, and whether it can see how much time has passed. Start with an effort sweep on your current model ( Tune effort ). From lowest to highest cost and capability, the current models are Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1 (the frontier model); Models overview has the full lineup and prices.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Compare models on cost per task 
text:
### Compare models on cost per task 
Compare models on cost per completed task, not per token, because you pay for completed tasks. For most agent workloads, start with Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort ( medium ).
A more capable model can finish a task with less work, which can offset much of the per-token premium. Anthropic measured this on the SWE-bench Pro 3 subset, whose scores are not comparable to the public leaderboard, priced as a customer is billed:
The following table lists the results:
| Benchmark | Model | Effort | Score | Cost |
| SWE-bench Pro 3 subset | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | high (default) | 87.6% of tasks solved | $0.11 USD per solved task |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Opus 5.5 | low | 87.4% of tasks solved | $0.12 USD per solved task |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Opus 5.5 | medium (default) | 92.8% of tasks solved | $0.22 USD per solved task |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Fable 5.1 | high (default) | 92.3% of tasks solved (a single run) | $1.19 USD per solved task |
| Internal agentic-coding benchmark 11 | Claude Opus 5.5 | medium (default) | 86.6% | $0.84 USD per attempt |
| Internal agentic-coding benchmark | Claude Fable 5.1 | medium | 84.2% (a single run) | $2.68 USD per attempt |
| GPQA Diamond 9 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | medium (default) | 85% accuracy, compared with 91% for each of Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 | About a twentieth of Claude Opus 5.5's cost per correct answer and about a tenth of Claude Sonnet 5.5's |
| Claude Managed Agents task set 25 , 79 tasks | Claude Haiku 5.5 | medium | 93% of attempts passed (a single run) | About $0.011 USD per passed attempt |
What to do.
- Start with Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort: on the SWE-bench Pro subset it matched Claude Fable 5.1 at its default, inside run-to-run noise, for about a fifth of the cost per solved task. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 both largely saturate the SWE-bench Pro subset. Use Claude Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when your evals on Claude Opus 5.5 at higher effort still fall short.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Compare models on cost per task 
text:
- At the other end, Claude Haiku 5.5 suits high-volume and latency-sensitive work with checkable outputs.
- Price every candidate in cost per completed task on your own traffic, including Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort and the frontier model at reduced effort. Each of Claude Opus 5.5's token prices, cache reads included, is twice Claude Sonnet 5.5's, but on the SWE-bench Pro subset Opus 5.5 at low solved about the same share of tasks as Sonnet 5.5 at its default, inside run-to-run noise, for about 7% more per solved task.
- The ranking flips by workload, and no price list tells you which way, so measure it on your own workload. On long research loops, Claude Fable 5.1 can do more work, not less, and so cost more per task (DeepResearch Bench II 7 ).
- Price the tail of your workload, not the median: compare models on the hardest tenth of your tasks, not the typical one.
The bill is decided by the tasks the cheaper model fails, because a failed task still bills its tokens, then the retry, then whatever the failure costs downstream. The tail is also where the money goes even when nothing fails. On a 20-problem WideSearch 1 run, two problems carried 43% of the spend:
The multi-model strategies exist to spend frontier intelligence on that tail without paying frontier rates for the rest.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Upgrade the model 
text:
### Upgrade the model 
If you are a model or two behind, the cheapest lever is the model string. In Anthropic's measurements , each newer model solved at least as many tasks as the one before it , usually for less per solved task . The chart plots recent Claude models on the SWE-bench Pro 3 subset, where every model ran through the same test setup, and on Terminal-Bench 3 20 ; the table lists what each upgrade changed:
| Benchmark | Upgrade | Effort | Score | Cost |
| SWE-bench Pro 3 subset | Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Claude Sonnet 5 | Default | 5 more points | 16% less per solved task |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Sonnet 5 to Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Default | About 10 more points | 87% less per solved task; 85% less at Claude Sonnet 5's prices |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Opus 5 to Claude Opus 5.5 | Default: high to medium | About the same: 91.9% to 92.8% of tasks solved | 78% less per solved task; about 69% less at Claude Opus 5's prices |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Fable 5 to Claude Fable 5.1 | Default | About the same score | 43% less per solved task |
| DeepResearch Bench II 7 | Claude Fable 5 to Claude Fable 5.1 | high | 2 to 3 more points on the 21 tasks where no attempt was cut short | 46% more per task on all 50 tasks |
| DeepResearch Bench II | Claude Fable 5 to Claude Fable 5.1 | low | 2 to 3 more points on the 21 tasks where no attempt was cut short | 94% more per task on all 50 tasks |
| Terminal-Bench 3 20 | Claude Opus 4.7 to Claude Opus 4.8 | high | From 7% to 15% of tasks solved | From $183 USD to $63 USD per solved task |
| Terminal-Bench 3 | Claude Opus 4.8 to Claude Opus 5 | high | From 15% to 41% of tasks solved | From $63 USD to $28 USD per solved task, a 56% saving |
| Claude Managed Agents task set 25 | Claude Haiku 4.5 to Claude Haiku 5.5 | As served; medium on Claude Haiku 5.5 | From 62% to 93% of attempts passed, one run per model | From $0.041 USD to about $0.010 USD in token cost per attempt; about 84% less per passed attempt |

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Upgrade the model 
text:
When it pays.
- Where older models already solve most tasks, the cost of each attempt decides the saving: on the SWE-bench Pro subset, Claude Opus 5.5 scores about the same as Claude Opus 5 for 78% less per solved task.
- Where older models mostly fail, the pass rate decides the saving: on Terminal-Bench 3 20 , the upgrade from Claude Opus 4.8 to Claude Opus 5 raises tasks solved from 15% to 41% and costs 56% less per solved task.
- Measure the upgrade on your own workload before assuming it saves. The saving is not guaranteed: on DeepResearch Bench II 7 , Claude Fable 5.1 costs more per task than Claude Fable 5 because the new model does more work per task there, although the input and output prices are the same and the cache read is 4x cheaper.
- Compare on cost per solved task, not per token: the same text costs about 30% more tokens on Claude 4.7 and later models, so a per-token comparison makes the newer models look more expensive by construction.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Tune effort 
text:
### Tune effort 
Sweep effort on your own workload before you add a second model. Lower effort costs less and is often faster, and how much accuracy it gives up depends on the task: on long-horizon coding, effort bought accuracy, and on research tasks it bought a lot in one measurement and nothing in another. The effort parameter governs how much thinking, tool calling, and self-verification the model does; high is the default on most models, and medium on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5.
The following table lists Anthropic's measurements on two benchmarks with current models; scores and costs are not comparable between the two benchmarks. Costs are per task, not per solved task as in Compare models on cost per task . Each score pools two runs on SWE-bench Pro and three on DeepResearch Bench II, unless its cell says otherwise:
| Benchmark | Model | Effort | Score | Cost per task |
| SWE-bench Pro 3 subset | Claude Opus 5.5 | low | 87.4% of tasks solved | $0.11 USD |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Opus 5.5 | medium (default) | 92.8% of tasks solved | $0.21 USD |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Opus 5.5 | high | 95.3% of tasks solved | $0.29 USD |
| SWE-bench Pro subset | Claude Opus 5.5 | xhigh | 96.7% of tasks solved (a single run) | $0.74 USD |
| DeepResearch Bench II 7 | Claude Fable 5.1 | low | Rubric score 66% | $4.48 USD |
| DeepResearch Bench II | Claude Fable 5.1 | high (default) | Rubric score 65% | $6.89 USD |
The following chart plots accuracy against cost per task for Claude Opus 5.5 on the SWE-bench Pro 3 subset:
The following chart plots rubric score against cost per task for Claude Fable 5.1 on DeepResearch Bench II 7 :
What to do.
- Sweep two or three effort levels on a sample of your own traffic, each in a separate session: changing top-level effort mid-session invalidates the cache and distorts the comparison. The curve is the baseline any multi-model strategy must beat ( step 2 of measuring on your own workload ).

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Tune effort 
text:
- On long-horizon coding, effort is a real tradeoff, which re-running failures at higher effort turns back into a saving. At medium , Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored about 7 points lower than at its default, high , on the SWE-bench Pro 3 subset for about 59% of the cost per task (2 runs each), and scored 62.7% compared with 77.8% on the internal agentic-coding benchmark 11 (1 attempt per task).
- At xhigh and max , Claude Sonnet 5.5 can start its own rounds of review after it finishes a task, which takes more time and tokens. To keep that work on the task, add the prompt under "Thoroughness at xhigh and max effort" in Prompting Claude Sonnet 5.5 to your system prompt.
- On research tasks, measure the model you ship. Claude Fable 5.1 scored nearly the same from low to high on DeepResearch Bench II; Claude Opus 5.5 scored 13.3 points lower at low than at medium on DRACO 21 . The two results come from different models on different benchmarks, so they show that the answer varies, not why.
- At low , Claude Opus 5.5's typical task took 84% less time than at medium on DRACO 21 , 30% less on HLE 22 , and 47% less on an internal set of physics problems 23 , and it scored 13.3, 3.4, and 14.0 points lower (3, 3, and 4 attempts per task).
- On an internal defect-search benchmark for work larger than one context window 8 , Claude Fable 5.1 took 15.2, 17.5, and 19.9 hours per run at low , medium , and high (3 runs each). To save time, also compare lower effort with the two changes in Show the model elapsed time : low effort saved more time, and the changes kept more of the score.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Re-run failures at higher effort 
text:
### Re-run failures at higher effort 
When a task's outcome is checkable, the cheapest policy on the effort curve is not a fixed setting: run every task at a low setting and re-run only the failures at a higher one.
Anthropic computed this policy task by task from the Claude Opus 5.5 effort runs on the SWE-bench Pro 3 subset in Tune effort :
In the following table, the re-run costs count the failed cheap attempts:
| Policy | Tasks solved | Cost per task |
| low , failures re-run at high | About 97% | About $0.17 USD |
| medium , failures re-run at high | About 97% | About $0.24 USD |
| Everything at high | 95.3% | $0.29 USD |
- At low , 13% of tasks failed. With those re-run at high , the pass rate was slightly higher than with everything at high , for a little over half the cost.
- Use this policy for the saving, not the lift. Most of the small lift is the second attempt: re-running the failures of one high run at high scores about the same, for more money.
Two conditions apply. First, you need a failure signal (here, the benchmark's own tests); a checker that passes bad work lets those failures through. Second, every first-pass failure takes two runs' worth of wall-clock time, so the saving is paid for in latency on the failures.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Set budgets and output caps 
text:
### Set budgets and output caps 
Two controls do two different jobs: a session budget caps what one Claude Managed Agents session can spend, and max_tokens caps the length of one response. Set each where it applies, with a workspace spend limit as the final backstop.
- Session budgets on Claude Managed Agents are a hard stop on spend. A session budget is a dollar cap on one session's list cost , which the platform meters for tokens, web searches, and session running time.
- At the cap, or a fraction past it, the session pauses with stop_reason: budget_reached ; raising the budget resumes it. It is platform-enforced and works on any model with a list price. Deployments apply the same budget to each session they start.
- max_tokens caps a single response, invisibly to the model, so lowering it does not make the model economize. The turns that needed the room are discarded and still billed. Retrying capped attempts rarely helps: at the same cap most of them fail again, and at a higher one you also pay for the wasted attempt.
- Set max_tokens to 64,000 for agentic work, or to 128,000, the maximum, when a single cut-off attempt is costly. Stream responses that large, treat stop_reason: max_tokens as a failure, and save money with effort, which the model can see.
The following table shows what each model solved and what a solved task cost at each cap on an internal repository-task benchmark 12 , one attempt per task, each model at its default effort. The rows at 16,384 average two runs, and the other rows are one run each:
| Model | max_tokens | Attempts ended by the cap | Tasks solved | Cost per solved task |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 16,384 | 25% | 57.6% | $5.38 USD at list prices |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 64,000 | 0% | 75.6% | $5.38 USD at list prices |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 128,000 | 0% | 68.9% | $5.94 USD at list prices |

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Set budgets and output caps 
text:
| Claude Fable 5.1 | 16,384 | 43% | 36.3% | $21.37 USD as billed |
| Claude Fable 5.1 | 64,000 | 0% | 58.5% | $21.53 USD as billed |
| Claude Fable 5.1 | 128,000 | 1% | 60.0% | $21.74 USD as billed |
Claude Opus 5.5 at 64,000 and 128,000: No attempt was cut off at either cap, so the cap does not explain why these two rows differ in tasks solved or in cost per solved task. Each row is one run.
Compare the caps within each model. The two models were run a month apart, and their costs are priced on different bases.
Ask for shorter answers. Output tokens cost five times input tokens on Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, and in an agent loop every token the model writes comes back as input on every later turn, so you pay for a long answer again and again.
In a measurement on an earlier model 26 , Anthropic ran a small agent that triages bug reports ( Trim input and context tokens ) under three final-answer instructions, three runs each, with the same model and tools:
- The original asked for two lines.
- The shorter variant asked for one.
- The longer variant asked for a memo with six headed sections.
The following chart plots the cost per run of each format:
All three scored within run-to-run noise of each other against the correct labels, so the formats differ in what you pay far more than in what they get right. Ask for the answer you will read, not the one that looks thorough.
On the internal repository tasks 12 , almost every turn finishes far below a 16,384-token cap. The rare long turn is what a higher cap buys :

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Show the model elapsed time 
text:
### Show the model elapsed time 
To make an agent finish sooner and cost less, tell it that time matters, and show it the elapsed time on every request. In Anthropic's measurement, the two changes cut the time of a single Claude Opus 5.5 agent at medium effort by 47% and its cost by 60% on the typical (median) DRACO 21 research task, and its average score was 4.1 points lower.
On HLE 22 and an internal physics set 23 , the typical task took 14% and 7% less time, and the physics score was 3.0 points lower. Lowering effort to low saved more time and cost than the changes did, and lost more score (reference 21). Check the score on your own tasks before you adopt the changes.
For working code, see the Claude Cookbook recipe Multi-agent teams under latency pressure and budgets , which applies both changes to a team of agents. To say that time matters in the system prompt instead, see Time signals for multiagent harnesses .
The following chart also plots a team, whose lead agent rarely started helpers, and a single agent at low effort:

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Combine models 
text:
## Combine models 
Tune one model before you add a second: sweep effort on your current model first, because most workloads end there, and if the sweep shows a gap, price the stronger model alone at low effort. Build a pairing only if it beats the single model's whole curve of score against spend. The multi-model results on this page were judged against the same model at lower effort and against the next model down running alone, which is the comparison to run on your own workload.
The following table compares the two strategies:
| Strategy | Control flow | Frontier model's role | Fits | Frontier cost scales with |
| Advisor | Smaller model runs the loop, escalates on demand | Consulted for plans and corrections | Serial work that is hard in spots, such as a coding agent's many turns between a few real decisions | How often the executor gets stuck |
| Orchestrator | Frontier model runs the loop, delegates the bulk work | Plans, dispatches, and synthesizes | Work that fans out across genuinely independent files, documents, or cases, especially more than one context window of it | How hard the pieces are to coordinate |

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Advisor strategy: escalate hard decisions 
text:
### Advisor strategy: escalate hard decisions 
An advisor can help only when the executor consults it.
In Anthropic's measurements on current models, the one pairing whose executor consulted often, on a coding benchmark, scored 1.7 points higher than the executor alone at the same effort, at the edge of run-to-run noise, for about 2.1 times the cost. Where the executor rarely or never consulted, the pairing scored within run-to-run noise of the executor alone, or lower.
To turn it on, add the advisor tool , a beta feature, to your request. On Claude Managed Agents, give the session an advisor . For Claude Code, see escalating hard decisions with the advisor tool .
The following table compares each pairing with its executor alone at the same effort:
| Benchmark | Score | Cost | Advisor consulted |
| Internal agentic-coding benchmark 11 | 90.1%, 1.7 points over the executor alone, at the edge of run-to-run noise | $2.92 USD per attempt, about 2.1 times the executor alone | About 1.4 times per attempt; 4% of attempts received no advice |
| GPQA Diamond 9 | Within run-to-run noise of the executor alone | 12% more per question for Claude Haiku 5.5, 25% more for Claude Sonnet 5.5 | On none of the 198 questions, in two runs each; no system prompt asked for consultations |
| Chartography 13 | 61.7, 7 points below the executor alone and beyond run-to-run noise | About the same as the executor alone | On 1 of 300 tasks |
- Internal agentic-coding benchmark. Claude Opus 5.5 at high , with a Claude Fable 5.1 advisor.
- GPQA Diamond. Claude Haiku 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 at each model's default ( medium and high ), with a Claude Opus 5.5 advisor.
- Chartography. Claude Opus 5.5 at low , with a Claude Fable 5.1 advisor.
The advisor can only hand over capability the executor lacks: on GPQA Diamond, Claude Sonnet 5.5 alone tied Claude Opus 5.5 alone at 91% with refusals counted as wrong, but only because Opus 5.5 refused six biology questions per run compared with Sonnet 5.5's one. On the questions each answered, Opus 5.5 led by about 2 points.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Advisor strategy: escalate hard decisions 
text:
On the coding benchmark, the pairing's gain is at the edge of run-to-run noise, and it lands about on Claude Opus 5.5's own effort curve, so the advisor bought about what more effort does. The following chart plots the pairing against that curve and Claude Fable 5.1's from August:
What to do.
- Measure the consult rate on your own tasks. The advisor tool's definition, about 1,000 prompt tokens per request, adds cost even when the executor never consults. With prompt caching , a multi-turn agent loop pays for the definition at the cache-read price after the first request, so this overhead matters most for short, single-request tasks.
- If the executor rarely consults, see Prompting for coding and agent tasks for system prompts that ask for consultations, and measure again after you add one. On 20 SWE-bench Pro 3 problems, the suggested prompt made no clear difference for Claude Sonnet 5.5.
- Restore the executor's effort if the consult rate collapses. In measurements on earlier models, one pairing that consulted on most tasks at the default effort consulted on few when effort was lowered, and then scored below the executor alone (SWE-bench Pro 3 ).
- Recheck at every model release, because releases move both the capability gap and the price ratio.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Orchestrator strategy: delegate bulk work 
text:
### Orchestrator strategy: delegate bulk work 
Delegation saved money in only two situations, in measurements with workers on Claude Sonnet 5, an earlier model:
- Routine work with a long cost tail (an easy slice of BrowseComp 4 )
- Work larger than one context window (an internal defect-search benchmark 8 )
When the work is one dependent chain, or fits in a single context without a long cost tail, the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead in every case measured, also on earlier models (the harder BrowseComp set and DeepWideSearch 6 ); independent external work reports the same pattern 5 .
To build an orchestrator, use multiagent orchestration in Claude Managed Agents: configure an orchestrator agent and worker agents that it can call, each with its own model.
The Model selection matrix lists Claude Haiku 5.5 for sub-agent tasks; before you use it as a worker, measure it on your own workload .
The following chart plots the defect-search benchmark's configurations by cost and score:
What to do.
- Routine work with a long cost tail: measure this case first, for accuracy as well as cost. The measurement behind it covers only problems that the delegated configuration answered correctly in every run (reference 4).
- Work larger than one context window: delegate partitions to workers. Lowering effort cannot help, because the bill is the reading itself: on the defect-search benchmark 8 , Claude Fable 5.1 alone cost $468 USD to $552 USD per run across its three effort settings and took 15 to 20 hours. With earlier-model workers, delegation cost less and finished sooner, for a lower score.

title: "Optimizing for cost and intelligence - Claude Platform Docs"
heading: Measure on your own workload 
text:
## Measure on your own workload 
Measure on your own workload: the numbers on this page reflect list prices at the time of measurement and will drift as models and prices change, and your escalation rate, how cleanly tasks split, and transcript length move them too. The method stays the same:
- Pull a few tasks from production logs, weighted like real traffic, and write outcome checks for each: tests pass, ticket closed, row count correct. Record cost per task beside the score.
- Baseline the model tiers across effort levels, not only the default, and plot score against spend. A multi-model configuration must beat the single model's whole curve.
- If the curve shows a gap effort can't close, add the multi-model strategy that fits and re-run the suite.
- Run the winner in shadow on a traffic slice before cutover, then keep the suite running.
How to price a task. Each response's usage has five priced token counts. Price each at its own rate: uncached input, 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes at 1.25x and 2x the input price, cache reads, and output. Sum them across the task's requests (the Usage and Cost API reports the aggregate). On Claude Haiku 5.5, price each request at the rates for its prompt length, counting cache reads and writes (see Long context pricing ).
The following example computes one request's cost at Claude Opus 5.5's list prices. Change the three prices for another model:

heading: Automate the search with the Claude API skill 
text:
### Automate the search with the Claude API skill 
Run the Claude API skill 's cost-optimize command before you search for savings. It profiles where your tokens go and applies the levers in order, caching first:
Claude Code
